about: The controlled list of concept tags. Every question's `concepts:` list must use ids from here. To add a concept, add an entry (id in lowercase-with-hyphens) and run `python3 tools/build.py`.

concepts.label: Decoder transformer pipeline
concepts.definition: The end-to-end path from context to next token: tokenize, embed, pass through the decoder stacks, produce probabilities, pick a token. The same basic architecture sits under Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.

concepts.label: Tokenization
concepts.definition: Splitting text into tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary and replacing each with its token ID (a number).

concepts.label: Token
concepts.definition: The unit a model reads and writes: a whole word, a piece of a word, or a symbol. Models predict tokens, not words.

concepts.label: Token embedding
concepts.definition: The learned vector (a long list of numbers) that a token ID is mapped to before the decoder stacks. One fixed embedding per token, whatever the sentence.

concepts.label: Semantic space
concepts.definition: The high-dimensional space embeddings live in, where location is meaning: related tokens sit near each other and directions can carry relationships (king - man + woman lands near queen).

concepts.label: Attention
concepts.definition: The part of each decoder stack that lets a token gather information from the other tokens in the context, moving its representation toward its meaning in this particular sentence.

concepts.label: MLP (multi-layer perceptron)
concepts.definition: The feed-forward part of each decoder stack. Its learned weights hold a compressed, lossy picture of the world (the "fuzzy JPEG") that it applies to each token's representation.

concepts.label: Decoder stack
concepts.definition: One block of attention followed by an MLP. A model runs many stacks in sequence, each refining the representation further.

concepts.label: Activation space
concepts.definition: The changing internal representations (activations) of tokens as they move through the stacks. Unlike the fixed token embedding, these depend on the context.

concepts.label: Recurrent depth (looping)
concepts.definition: Running the same decoder stack or block more than once so a representation gets another pass ("a second bite of the apple"), adding computation without adding parameters.

concepts.label: Probability distribution over tokens
concepts.definition: The model's output at each step: a probability for every token in its vocabulary (the softmax at the end of the pipeline).

concepts.label: Next-token prediction
concepts.definition: The single job a language model is trained to do and does at run time: predict what token comes next given the context.

concepts.label: Sampling and temperature
concepts.definition: How one token is chosen from the probability distribution. Temperature reshapes the distribution: higher means more varied, lower means more predictable.

concepts.label: Autoregression
concepts.definition: Generating one token at a time and feeding each chosen token back into the context for the next step, so every choice shapes what follows.

concepts.label: Parameter
concepts.definition: A single learned number (weight) in the model. The parameter count is how many there are; they are fixed once training ends.

concepts.label: Model size
concepts.definition: How big a model is (parameter count, width of the embedding space, number of decoder stacks) and what bigger does and does not buy you.

concepts.label: Learned knowledge
concepts.definition: What a model knows from training and how it is stored: compressed and approximate, not a searchable database of facts or a copy of its sources.

concepts.label: Hallucination
concepts.definition: Fluent output that is wrong. The model always produces the likely-sounding continuation; sometimes likely-sounding is not true.

concepts.label: Context
concepts.definition: Everything the model sees for a given step: system instructions, the conversation so far, uploaded files, tool results and its own output so far. The most important lever you have.

concepts.label: Context length
concepts.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can hold in its context at once (the context window), and what happens as you approach it.

concepts.label: Grounding with documents
concepts.definition: Putting the relevant source material into the context so the answer draws on it rather than on the model's lossy memory, and why irrelevant material does not help.

concepts.label: Pre-training
concepts.definition: The first, largest training stage: next-token prediction over a huge body of text (and sometimes images), producing a base model.

concepts.label: Self-supervised learning
concepts.definition: Training where the answer key comes from the data itself, such as hiding the next token and asking the model to guess it.

concepts.label: Post-training
concepts.definition: Training after pre-training that turns a base model into an assistant: supervised fine-tuning on example responses, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and similar methods.

concepts.label: Alignment
concepts.definition: Work to make a model's behavior helpful, honest and safe, such as refusing harmful requests, and why that behavior is never perfectly reliable.

concepts.label: Training vs. inference
concepts.definition: Training changes the weights; inference (using the model) does not. A model can respond differently to new context without learning anything.

concepts.label: Thinking / reasoning
concepts.definition: A model generating hidden tokens that work through a problem before its visible answer. Same architecture and same next-token mechanism, just more tokens spent first.

concepts.label: Thinking budget and effort
concepts.definition: The limit on how many thinking tokens a model may spend (the effort setting in Claude), and matching that budget to the task.

concepts.label: Choosing a model
concepts.definition: Picking a model tier (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable, or another vendor's equivalents): the smallest model that does the job correctly.

concepts.label: Inference speed and hardware
concepts.definition: How fast tokens are produced (GPUs, specialized chips, local laptops) and why taking in a prompt is faster than writing an answer.

concepts.label: KV cache
concepts.definition: The stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so each new token does not recompute the whole context.

concepts.label: Cost, usage and footprint
concepts.definition: Usage limits and credits, and the energy and environmental cost of bigger models and bigger budgets.

concepts.label: Multimodality
concepts.definition: Models that work with images, audio or video as well as text, whether trained jointly (native) or given a separate adapter.

concepts.label: History of AI
concepts.definition: The eras of AI (problem solvers, expert systems, machine learning, deep learning) and where transformers, generative AI and agents fit.

concepts.label: AGI (artificial general intelligence)
concepts.definition: What AGI has been taken to mean, how definitions and levels frameworks differ, and the argument about whether a milestone has passed.

concepts.label: Agent
concepts.definition: A model plus tools plus autonomy: a system that can take actions in a loop toward a goal, not just reply once.

concepts.label: Chat vs. agent
concepts.definition: The difference between a plain chat and an agent surface (Cowork, Claude Code): same model, different access, tools and ability to act.

concepts.label: Harness
concepts.definition: The software around the model that manages context, carries out tool calls, enforces permissions and returns results. The model proposes; the harness executes.

concepts.label: Tool
concepts.definition: A capability the harness can run on the model's behalf, such as reading a file, running a command or searching, with the result returned into context.

concepts.label: Connector (MCP)
concepts.definition: An add-on that gives an agent access to an outside system, often through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

concepts.label: File system
concepts.definition: The folders and files an agent can read and write, and why working through files lets an agent handle projects bigger than its context.

concepts.label: Memory
concepts.definition: How information persists beyond one context window: notes, working records, remembered preferences and project files, and keeping them accurate.

concepts.label: Context management
concepts.definition: Keeping a long task's context useful: compaction and summaries, starting fresh chats, and keeping original evidence available.

concepts.label: Subagent
concepts.definition: A fresh agent given a focused assignment and just the background it needs, so it starts with a clean context.

concepts.label: Permissions and safety
concepts.definition: What an agent is allowed to do (access controls, sandboxes, approvals) and judging whether shared code or broad access is safe.

concepts.label: Computer use
concepts.definition: Agents that operate a computer's screen, mouse and keyboard, and why that remains hard.

concepts.label: Directing an agent
concepts.definition: Telling an agent what you need: stating the problem and goal (a "North Star"), constraints and acceptance criteria rather than step-by-step instructions.

concepts.label: Verification
concepts.definition: Checking that work actually happened and is correct (reading back the result, inspecting the file) rather than trusting a claim that it did.

concepts.label: Agent skill
concepts.definition: A folder of reusable instructions (and optionally scripts and references) that an agent loads when a task calls for it.

concepts.label: Skill structure
concepts.definition: What goes in a skill folder: SKILL.md with its name and description, references/, scripts/, assets/, and what stays loaded versus loaded on demand.

concepts.label: Skill selection
concepts.definition: How an agent decides which skill to use from its name and description, and how vague, overlapping or conflicting skills go wrong.

concepts.label: Skill scope
concepts.definition: Where a skill lives and who can use it: a personal skill that follows you across projects versus a project skill tied to one project's conventions.

concepts.label: Skill Creator
concepts.definition: The skill for building, improving and testing other skills.

concepts.label: Evaluating a skill
concepts.definition: Testing whether a skill helps: comparing runs with and without it on the same inputs, criteria set in advance, varied test cases, the cheaper model it will run on.

concepts.label: Sharing skills
concepts.definition: Moving skills between people and hosts: repositories, READMEs, portability across providers, and what breaks when a skill is copied.

concepts.label: Classification and decision models
concepts.definition: Choosing among fixed options (labels) rather than writing open-ended text, and when a specialized decision model fits better.

concepts.label: Calibration
concepts.definition: Whether stated probabilities match how often things actually happen: of events given 80%, about 80% should occur.

concepts.label: Decisions under risk
concepts.definition: Combining probabilities with costs (false alarms, misses, what each outcome costs) to choose an action, not just the most likely outcome.

concepts.label: Feedback and rubrics
concepts.definition: Grading against a rubric and writing feedback that names what was missed and how to fix it.

concepts.label: Data privacy
concepts.definition: Keeping personal and student data out of code, prompts and repositories, and building tools that look it up only when needed.

concepts.label: Class demonstration
concepts.definition: Questions about a specific in-class demonstration or case study (for example seat-minder or the grading demo) rather than a general concept.

concepts.label: Course logistics
concepts.definition: How this course runs: quizzes, appeals, labs and exercises.
